title: Oil, gas and offshore, 18 days of posts

clusters.text: The Houthis threatened to strike Saudi Aramco's headquarters and Riyadh refinery if Saudi Arabia hits Sanaa's oil depot.
clusters.verdict_basis: Reuters reporting, carried by SCMP and US News, says the Houthis threatened a "harsh and painful" response to Saudi-led strikes on Sanaa. It says spokesman Yahya Saree named the Saudi Aramco headquarters in Dhahran and an oil refinery in Riyadh as possible targets. The threat followed the coalition's evacuation order for the Yemen Petroleum Company's Sabah (al-Sabah) fuel depot on Sanaa's outskirts, which the coalition then struck. Al Jazeera likewise describes the threat as a reaction to that order. The claim's wording is accurate, though it is now incomplete. Al Jazeera, France 24 and the Korea Times report that the Houthis then claimed attacks on Aramco in Dhahran and on a Riyadh refinery, and Saudi officials confirmed a strike on an Aramco building in Dhahran. The claim has no obvious connection to Texas politics. I judged only its accuracy.

lanes.label: Texas oil as security and affordability

clusters.text: Saudi Arabia struck Sanaa's Al-Sabaha oil depot, triggering Houthi retaliation threats.
clusters.verdict_basis:
The strike is well documented. 
The Saudi-led coalition confirmed on Tuesday (Oct 13) that it had targeted a Yemeni oil company facility in Sanaa.
 
Coalition spokesman Maj Gen Turki al-Maliki said the Houthis used the Yemen Petroleum Company's al-Sabaha facility to fuel their war effort.
 The BBC (via Yahoo), Al Jazeera, the Times of Israel and France 24 all report it. The Houthi threats are also documented. 
Houthi spokesman Yahya Saree warned that any strike on Sanaa would meet a "harsh and painful" reprisal on Riyadh.
 
The Houthis then reportedly targeted an Aramco administrative building in Dhahran, according to Saudi SPA.
 
Saree also said operations toward Saudi depths would continue, targeting airports and oil facilities.


Two nuances. The strike came from the Saudi-led coalition, which is the usual shorthand for Saudi Arabia. The first Houthi threats were made in response to the coalition's evacuation warning, before the strike itself, so "triggering" is loosely worded. The Houthis did follow up with more threats and an actual attack after the strike. None of this changes the claim's substance. The Texas oil-policy context has no bearing on it.

lanes.label: Texas oil as security and affordability

clusters.text: The IEA says global diesel shortages will last well into 2027.
clusters.verdict_basis:
The IEA's October 2026 Oil Market Report (published Oct 14) has a section headed "Gasoil and diesel market tightness set to extend into 2027." 
The section covers diesel market tightness extending into 2027.
 Reuters, via BOE Report, reported that 
constrained diesel supplies could persist well into next year
. CNBC reported that the IEA 
said supply would remain tight into the latter half of 2027
, and that 
replenishing lost inventories may not begin before the second half of 2027
. The claim's wording ("global diesel shortages will last well into 2027") is slightly firmer than the IEA's hedged language ("could persist," "likely to persist"). It also describes a global market tightness, not a Texas matter. The core attribution, the timing and the "well into 2027" phrasing all match the IEA and the news coverage, so the gist is accurate.

lanes.label: Texas oil as security and affordability

clusters.text: Democrats have no proposal or plan to lower prices, especially gas.
clusters.verdict_basis:
The records contradict the claim as worded. The Texas Tribune's Oct. 8, 2026 candidate guide (via Yahoo) says Democratic governor nominee Gina Hinojosa 
has called for a pause on the state and federal gas taxes
. It says Senate nominee James Talarico 
has called for a pause on federal gas and diesel taxes and an end to the war with Iran
. The Dallas Morning News and WFAA report the same Hinojosa and Talarico gas-tax proposals. At the federal level, Sens. Mark Kelly and Richard Blumenthal introduced the Gas Prices Relief Act, which 
would temporarily suspend the 18.4 cents-per-gallon federal gas tax through October 1, 2026
. Rep. Dina Titus introduced a bill on Oct. 15 on fuel-efficiency standards, with the stated aim of countering high gas prices. Experts quoted by the Tribune 
widely pan proposals to suspend the state and federal gas tax
, and Republicans such as Gov. Abbott's office and Sen. Cornyn have opposed them. Critics can fairly dispute whether the proposals would work, but "no proposal or plan" is inaccurate because Democrats have made specific, documented proposals.

lanes.label: Texas oil as security and affordability

clusters.text: Democrats created the cost of living crisis.
clusters.verdict_basis: The claim is a sweeping causal and partisan statement, and the records don't support it as worded. The Congressional Research Service says the 2021–22 inflation began with COVID-19 supply disruptions, was worsened by the war in Ukraine, and was also fed by "unprecedented fiscal and monetary stimulus" (https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47273). Stimulus was passed under presidents of both parties. Economists disagree about how much each factor mattered: Richmond Fed and New York Fed work stresses supply-side factors, while an MIT Sloan summary of new research emphasizes federal spending (https://www.richmondfed.org/publications/research/econ_focus/2022/q3_feature2, https://mitsloan.mit.edu/ideas-made-to-matter/federal-spending-was-responsible-2022-spike-inflation-research-shows). Some Democratic-backed spending is a defensible contributor, but no source says one party "created" the crisis. For Texas specifically, the Dallas Fed attributes rising home-insurance costs to construction costs, climate risk and reinsurance costs, not to one party (https://www.dallasfed.org/research/swe/2026/swe2609). The claim also names no specific policy, so it can't be tested against the oil-and-gas

clusters.text: The Trump administration has secured every federal permit for the $54 billion Alaska LNG pipeline.
clusters.verdict_basis:
The Permitting Council reported that 
NOAA renewed the final permit, completing federal approvals for the project on December 10
 (2025). It also called this 
the 21st and very last federal permitting action for Alaska LNG
. Natural Gas Intelligence, a trade outlet, likewise reports that the project 
was approved by FERC in 2020 and has all of its federal permits
. Most of the permit renewals and updated biological opinions were handled in 2025, when 
the sponsor reactivated the project's FAST-41 coverage in February 2025
. That fits the credit to the Trump administration, though the original FERC approval dates from 2020, in Trump's first term.

The $54 billion figure is a loose fit. It is the amount Trump said South Korea would invest. 
Official cost estimates run from $44.5 billion to $54.5 billion
, so $54 billion is within that range. South Korea's industry minister 
told reporters his government had agreed neither to $54 billion nor to an investment at all
. Also, 
Glenfarne has yet to announce a final investment decision
, so permits do not mean the project is funded or that construction has started. The claim says only that permits are secured, and that is accurate. A separ

clusters.text: Over the past year fuel oil rose 74.2%, gasoline 34.2%, airfares 22.4%, and inflation was 3.7%, per BLS.
clusters.verdict_basis:
The BLS September 2026 CPI release, published October 14, 2026, matches the claim. Over the 12 months ending September, 
gasoline rose 34.2%
 and 
airline fares rose 22.4%
. The all-items index 
rose 3.7 percent for the 12 months ending September
. A BLS "Economics Daily" piece gives the same set: 
fuel oil up 74.2 percent and airline fares up 22.4 percent
, with 
all items up 3.7 percent
. CNBC reports the same gasoline and fuel oil figures (
34.2% for gas and 74.2% for fuel oil
). These are national CPI numbers, not Texas-specific. They are also not seasonally adjusted, and the claim doesn't say so.

lanes.label: Texas oil as security and affordability

clusters.text: Over the past year car insurance, medical products, used cars and dairy prices fell.
clusters.verdict_basis:
The BLS September 2026 CPI release (published Oct. 14, 2026) shows that all four categories fell over the 12 months ending in September, on a national basis. Motor vehicle insurance fell 5.0%, used cars and trucks fell 1.5%, and dairy and related products fell 0.7%, per the 
BLS Economics Daily table
. 
Medical care commodities fell 3.3%
 in BLS Table 1. The release breaks that down as 
medicinal drugs −3.4% and medical equipment and supplies −1.3%
. "Medical products" is a loose label for that category, but it fits. The claim doesn't say these declines were offset elsewhere. 
The all-items index rose 3.7% over the same period
, and 
gasoline rose 34.2%
. The figures are U.S. city averages, not Texas-specific, and the claim doesn't say they are. Regional BLS data are broadly consistent: 
in the South region dairy was down 2.8% and used cars down 1.3%
.

clusters.text: Don Henley wants Texas to turn blue.
clusters.verdict_basis:
The claim is vague, but it matches the reporting. A Houston Chronicle piece published Oct. 3, 2026 says 
Henley "really wants to see his native Texas turn blue for the first time in more than 30 years."
 It adds that he is 
the number one donor to Democratic candidates for lieutenant governor, agriculture commissioner and the Railroad Commission
, and that he is a major backer of the Lone Star Rising super PAC supporting James Talarico's Senate bid. The Chronicle's donor pages show 
$165,500 to Vikki Goodwin as of Sept. 24
 and 
$31,000 to Railroad Commission nominee Jon Rosenthal
. The Chronicle also notes that 
he doesn't often talk about his politics in interviews, but has made clear he's a Democrat
. The "wants" is therefore inferred by the Chronicle from his donations and party affiliation, not taken from a direct statement by Henley. Because that inference is well supported by campaign-finance records, I rate the claim supported.

lanes.label: Industry money, capture, conflicts of interest

clusters.text: The Trump administration is using the Defense Production Act to expand Delek's Tyler refinery.
clusters.verdict_basis: Reuters (Oct 13) reported that Vice President JD Vance, speaking in Tyler, said the administration, working with Delek, "has used the Defense Production Act" and will expand the Tyler refinery. The Hill, Fox 7 Austin, the Tyler Morning Telegraph and Bloomberg (via Rigzone) carried the same quote. This matches the claim's wording: the administration, the DPA, Delek and the Tyler refinery. Two caveats apply. First, the evidence is a public announcement by an official. Reuters said the White House and Delek did not immediately say how much funding is involved or how much capacity will grow, and energynews.pro found no public document describing the DPA action. Second, the reports describe an expansion that is announced or planned, so "is using" is a fair paraphrase of Vance's statement but not proof of a completed action. A White House official told Bloomberg that Tyler is one of several refineries the administration is working with on DPA funds. The claim's central assertion is accurately reported.

clusters.text: South Korea and the US announced a $22.3 billion, 6.47 GW gas plant (Project Star) in La Salle County, Texas, larger than Texas's nuclear plants combined.
clusters.verdict_basis:
The joint announcement by NextEra Energy, Related Companies and Lewis Energy Group (
Lewis Energy Group supplies the land, produced water and gas
) describes Project Star as a $22.3 billion energy campus in Encinal, La Salle County. The Commerce Department and the Korean government announced it. 
It is planned to include 6.47 GW of natural gas generation to support an adjacent 5 GW data center campus.
 Coverage describes it as the first formally selected project under the US–Korea strategic investment framework (
dmc-education summary
). On the comparison, Texas has two nuclear plants, South Texas Project (
2,709 MW
) and Comanche Peak (
2,430 MW
). Cleanview puts their combined capacity at 
5,139 MW
, and other estimates are about 4.9 to 5.1 GW, so 6.47 GW is larger than both plants combined. One caveat is that this is a planned plant, with 
first-phase operations expected in 2029 and full operations in 2032
. The claim says "announced," which fits that. It does not say the plant is built.
